bio.en: Mike Krieger is the Chief Product Officer at Anthropic, maker of Claude, and the co-founder of Instagram, one of the most influential product thinkers in tech.
bio.zh: 迈克·克里格（Mike Krieger）是 Anthropic（Claude 的开发者）的首席产品官，也是 Instagram 的联合创始人，是科技界最具影响力的产品思考者之一。

summary.en: Mike reveals that over half - now ~70% - of Anthropic's pull requests are generated by Claude Code, forcing a re-architecture of their merge queue. He describes the Claude Code team building Claude Code in a self-improving loop as the most futuristic way of working. The episode offers a front-row view of product-building inside a leading AI lab.
summary.zh: 迈克透露，Anthropic 超过一半（如今约 70%）的合并请求由 Claude Code 生成，迫使他们重新架构合并队列。他描述 Claude Code 团队用 Claude Code 自我迭代地构建自身，是"最具未来感"的工作方式。本期让人近距离看到领先 AI 实验室内部的产品构建。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: 90% of your code roughly is written by AI now.
turns.zh: 如今，你们90%的代码都是由人工智能编写的。

turns.speaker: Mike Krieger
turns.en: The team that works in the most futuristic way is the Claude Code team. They're using Claude Code to build Claude Code in a very self-improving kind of way. We really rapidly became bottlenecked on other things like our merge queue. We had to completely re-architect it because so much more code was being written and so many more pull requests were being submitted. Over half of our pull requests are Claude Code generated. Probably at this point it's probably over 70% that it just completely blew out the expectations of it.
turns.zh: 采用最具未来感工作方式的团队当属Claude Code团队。他们正以一种自我进化的方式，利用Claude Code来构建Claude Code。我们的合并队列曾一度陷入瓶颈，不得不彻底重构整个架构，因为编写的代码量激增，提交的拉取请求数量也急剧增加。我们超过半数的拉取请求都是由Claude Code生成的。目前这个比例可能已超过70%，完全超出了我们的预期。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You guys are at the edge of where things are heading.
turns.zh: 你们正站在时代前沿。

turns.speaker: Mike Krieger
turns.en: I had the very bizarre experience of I had two tabs open. It was AI 2027, and my product strategy, and it was this moment where I'm like, "Wait, am I the character in the story?"
turns.zh: 我曾有过非常奇特的体验——同时打开两个标签页，一个是AI 2027，另一个是我的产品策略。就在那一刻，我突然意识到：“等等，我难道成了故事里的主角？”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It feels like ChatGPT is just winning in consumer mind share. How does that inform the way you think about product, strategy, and mission?
turns.zh: ChatGPT似乎正在消费者心目中赢得口碑。这对你们的产品、战略和使命规划有何启示？

turns.speaker: Mike Krieger
turns.en: I think there's room for several generationally important companies to be built in AI right now. How do we figure out what we want to be when we grow up versus what we currently aren't or wish that we were or see other players in the space being?
turns.zh: 我认为当下AI领域有空间诞生几家具有时代意义的巨头企业。我们该如何区分理想中的自己与现实中的自己，以及与同行公司的差距？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What's something that you've changed your mind about what AI is capable of and where AI is heading?
turns.zh: 有没有哪件事让你重新认识了AI的能力或发展方向？

turns.speaker: Mike Krieger
turns.en: I had this notion coming in like, "Yes, these models are great, but are they able to have an independent opinion?" And it's actually really flipped for me only in the last month.
turns.zh: 我曾有这样的疑问："这些模型固然出色，但它们能形成独立的判断吗？"但就在过去一个月里，我的看法彻底改变了。

turns.speaker: Mike Krieger
turns.en: Thank you. Not that we're tracking.
turns.zh: 谢谢。不过我们倒没特意追踪过这些数据。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's right. So let me just ask you this. So you've been at Anthropic for about a year. What's something that you've changed your mind about from before you joined Anthropic to today about what AI is capable of and where AI is heading?
turns.zh: 没错。接下来我想问你一个问题——你在Anthropic工作了一年，与加入前相比，你对AI的能力和发展方向有了哪些新的认识？

turns.speaker: Mike Krieger
turns.en: Two things. One is like a pace and timeline question. The other one is a capability question. So maybe I'll take the second one first. I had this notion coming in, yes, these models are great, they're going to be able to produce code, they're going to be able to write hopefully in your voice eventually, but are they able to sort of have an independent opinion? And it's actually really flipped for me only in the last month and only with Opus 4 where my go-to product strategy partner is Claude. And it has been basically for that full year where I'll write an initial strategy, I'll share it with Claude basically, and I'll have it, look at it. And in the past it's pretty anodyne kind of comments that it would leave, "Oh, have you thought about this?" And it's like, "Yeah, I thought about that." And Opus 4, I was working on some strategy for our second half of the year was the first one. (00:05:51): It was like Opus 4 combined with our advanced research. But it really went out for a while and it came back and I was like, you really looked at it in a new way. And so that's a thing that I've maybe I didn't feel like it would never be able to do that, but I wasn't sure how soon it'd be able to come up with something where I look at it, I'm like, yep, that is a new angle that I hadn't been looking at before and I'm going to incorporate that immediately into how I think about it. So that's probably the biggest shift that I've had is, I don't know about independence is the right word, but creativity and sort of novelty of thought relative to how I'm thinking about things. But in the timeline, one, it's so interesting because I was sitting next to Dario yesterday and he's like, "I keep making these predictions and people keep laughing at me. And then they come true." (00:06:31): And it's funny to have this happen over and over again and he is like, not all of them are going to be right. But even I think as of last year he was talking about we're at 50% on SWE-Bench, which is this benchmark around how well the models are at coding. He's like, "I think we'll be at 90% by the end of 2025 or something like that." And sure enough, we're at about 72 now with the new models and we're at 50% when he made that prediction. And it's continued to scale pretty much as predicted. And so I've taken the timelines a lot more seriously now. And I don't know if you read AI 2027-
turns.zh:
有两点。一是关于进度和时间线的问题。另一个是关于能力的问题。或许我先讲第二个。我刚加入时有这样的想法：这些模型很棒，能生成代码，最终或许能用你的语气写作，但它们能形成独立的观点吗？直到最近一个月，我才真正意识到这个转变。特别是Opus 4版本，我的首席产品策略伙伴Claude让我看到了全新的可能性。
过去一年里，我会写一份初步策略，与Claude分享，然后再审视。但过去的反馈通常比较平淡，比如“你考虑过这个吗？”而Opus 4版本让我在第二季度策略制定时，首次真正感受到Claude的深度参与。（00:05:51）：Opus 4与我们的先进研究相结合的成果，曾一度搁置，但后来又被重新启用。当我再次审视时，发现Claude以全新的视角进行了分析。这让我意识到，虽然我从前认为AI无法实现这种洞察，但我没料到它能这么快就产生这样的创新思维。时间线方面，去年我坐在Dario旁边，他说：“我老是做出预测，结果人们都嘲笑我。但最后这些预测都成真了。”（00:06:31）：这种循环往复很有趣。他说并非所有预测都能准确，但去年他就提到SWE-Bench（衡量模型编码能力的基准测试）的成绩达到50%。他当时预测2025年底能达到90%。而现在新模型已经达到72%，而他预测时是50%。整体进展基本符合预期。所以现在我对时间线预期的重视度大增了。你读过《AI 2027》报告吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I have, it made by heart race.
turns.zh: 读过，那本书让我心跳加速。

turns.speaker: Mike Krieger
turns.en: And I had the very bizarre experience of I had two tabs open, it was AI 2027 and my product strategy. And it was this moment where I'm like, "Wait, am I the character in the story? How much is this converging?" But you read that and you're like, "Oh, 2027, that's years away if you're like no, mid 2025." And things continue to improve and the models continue to be able to do more and more and they're able to act agentically and they're able to have memory and they're able to act over time. So I think my confidence in the timelines and I don't know exactly how they manifest it definitely just solidified over the last year.
turns.zh: 当时我经历了一件非常奇怪的事——我打开了两个标签页，一个是AI 2027项目，另一个是我的产品策略。就在那一刻，我突然意识到：“等等，我难道成了故事里的角色？这种融合程度究竟有多高？”但当你读到相关内容时，又会觉得：“哦，2027年？如果你现在是2025年中期，那还有好多年呢。”技术在不断进步，模型的能力越来越强，它们能自主行动、具备记忆功能、随时间演进。正因如此，我对技术发展的时间线信心倍增，尽管具体实现路径尚不明朗，但过去一年里这种信心确实更加坚定了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow. I wasn't expecting to go down that that paper was scary. And I'm curious just I guess I can't help but ask just thoughts on just how do we avoid the scary scenario that paper paints of where AI getting really smart goes?
turns.zh: 哇。我没想到那篇论文描绘的未来如此可怕。我很好奇，不妨问问大家，如何避免论文中提到的AI变得极其智能的恐怖场景？

turns.speaker: Mike Krieger
turns.en: Yeah, this maybe ties into, I've been here a year, why did I join Anthropic? I was watching the models get better and even you could see it in early 2024, and looking at my kids, I'm like, "All right, they're going to grow up in a world with AI. It's unavoidable." Where can I maximally apply my time to nudge things towards going well? And I mean that's a lot of what people think about across the industry, especially at Anthropic. And so I think coming to an agreement and a shared framework and understanding of what does going well look like? What is the kind of human AI relationship that we want? (00:08:36): How will we know along the way? What do we need to build and develop and research along the way? I think those are all the kind of key questions. And some of those are product questions and some of those are research and interpretability questions, but for me it was the strongest reason to join was okay. I think there's a lot of contribution that Anthropic can have around nudging things to go better. And if I can have a part to play there, let's do it.
turns.zh: 是啊，这或许关乎我为何加入Anthropic的原因。我在这里工作了一年，最初为何选择加入？早在2024年初，我就目睹了模型能力的飞跃。看着我的孩子们，我心想：“好吧，他们将在AI盛行的世界中成长，这是不可避免的。”那么，我该如何最大限度地利用时间，让事情朝着好的方向发展？这正是业界，尤其是Anthropic内部许多人都在思考的问题。所以我认为关键在于达成共识，建立共同框架，理解理想的AI与人类关系应是怎样的？我们希望看到怎样的AI与人类共存模式？（00:08:36）：如何在过程中验证成果？需要开展哪些研发和研究工作？这些都是核心问题。其中一些是产品层面的问题，另一些是研究和可解释性层面的问题。但对我来说，最重要的加入理由是——Anthropic在推动事物朝着积极方向发展方面能够发挥重要作用。如果我能为此贡献一份力量，那就义不容辞了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that answer. Speaking of kids, so you've got two kids, I've got a young kid, he's just about to turn two. I'm curious just what skills you're encouraging your kids to build as this AI becomes more and more of our future and some jobs will be changed and just what advice do you have?
turns.zh: 我很欣赏你的回答。说到孩子，你有两个孩子，我也有个小儿子，快两岁了。我想问问你，随着AI日益融入未来，某些工作岗位将被取代，你会鼓励孩子们培养哪些技能？对此你有什么建议？

turns.speaker: Mike Krieger
turns.en: We have this breakfast feed breakfast with the kids every morning and sometimes some question will come up, something about physics and our oldest kid's almost six, but they ask funny questions about the solar system or physics or in a 6-year-old way and before we reach for Claude, because at first my instinct is like, "Oh, I wonder how Claude will do this question." And we started changing, "Well, how would we find out?" And the answer can't just be we'll ask Claude, all right, well, we could do this experiment, we could have this thing. So I think nurturing curiosity and still having a sense of, I don't know, the scientific process sounds grandiose to instill in a 6-year-old, but that process of discovery and asking questions and then systematically working right through, I think will still be important. And of course AI will be an incredible tool for helping resolve large parts of that, but that process of inquiry I think is still really important and independent thought. (00:10:11): My favorite moment with my kid, because she's very headstrong, our 6-year-old, she said something and I wasn't sure if it was true. It was, oh, is that coral is an animal or corals alive? I don't even remember what the details of it. And I was like, "I don't know if that's true." And she's like, "It's definitely true, dad." I'm like, "All right, let's ask Claude on this one." And she's like, "You can ask Claude, but I know I'm right." And I'm like I love that. I want that kind of level of not just delegating all of your cognition to the AI because it won't always get it right. And also it kind of short circuits any kind of independent thought. So the skill of asking questions, inquiry and independent thinking, I think those are all the pieces. What that looks like from a job or occupation perspective, I'm just keeping an open mind and I'm sure that'll radically change between now and then.
turns.zh: 我们每天早上都会和孩子们一起享用早餐，有时会出现一些问题——比如关于物理学的疑问。我们的大儿子快六岁了，但他们会以六岁孩子的方式提出有趣的问题，比如关于太阳系或物理学的疑问。在我们还没来得及求助克劳德（Claude）之前（因为起初我的直觉是：“哦，我好奇克劳德会怎么回答这个问题。”），我们就会开始思考：“那我们该怎么查证呢？”答案不能只是“我们去问克劳德”——好吧，我们可以做这个实验，或者准备这个工具。所以我认为培养好奇心，同时保持对科学研究过程的理解听起来很宏大，但这种探索、提问、然后系统性地推进的过程，我认为仍然很重要。当然，人工智能将成为帮助解决其中大部分问题的绝佳工具，但这种探究的过程和独立思考仍然非常重要。（00:10:11）：我和孩子最喜欢的时刻，因为她非常固执，我们的六岁女儿，她说了一些东西，我不确定是否正确。是的，哦，珊瑚是动物还是活着的？我甚至不记得具体细节了。我当时说：“我不确定这是不是真的。”她说：“爸爸，这绝对是真的。”我说：“好吧，那我们去问问克劳德吧。”她说：“你可以问克劳德，但我知道我是对的。” 我很喜欢这一点。我不想把所有的认知都交给人工智能，因为它并不总是能回答正确。另外，这还会阻碍独立思考的能力。所以提问、探究和独立思考的技能，我认为这些都是关键。从工作或职业的角度来看，我保持开放的心态，我相信这在未来会发生巨大的变化。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's interesting. Tobias Lütke, Shopify CEO, on the podcast and he had the same answer for what he's encouraging his kids to develop is curiosity. And so it's interesting that's a common thread.
turns.zh: 有趣的是，Shopify CEO 托拜厄斯·卢特克（Tobias Lütke）在播客中也回答了同样的问题，他鼓励孩子们培养的也是好奇心。有趣的是，这是一个共同的主题。

turns.speaker: Mike Krieger
turns.en: The K through eight school our kid goes through had an AI and education expert come in and I had a very low bar or a very low expectation of what this conversation was going to be like. And actually I think it went over most of the people in the audience's heads because he was like, "All right, well let me take you all the way back to Claude Shannon in information theory." And I could see people's eyes going, "What did I sign up for and why am I hearing this school auditorium hearing about information theory?" But he did a really nice job I think of also just imagining there will be different jobs and we don't know what those jobs are going to be and so what are the skills and techniques and remain open mindedness around what the exact way we recombine those things. And even those will probably change three times between now and when they're 18.
turns.zh: 我们孩子上的是 K-8 年级的学校，有位人工智能和教育专家来做讲座。我对这次讲座的期望很低，觉得内容会很枯燥。但实际上，我觉得大多数听众都听得一头雾水，因为他一开始就说：“好吧，让我带你们回溯到克劳德·香农的信息论。”我能看到人们眼中流露出的困惑：“我报名参加的是什么活动？为什么我在学校礼堂听信息论？” 但我认为他做得很好，既设想了未来可能出现的不同职业，又强调了保持开放心态的重要性，思考如何重新组合这些技能和技术。甚至这些技能和技术在孩子们 18 岁之前可能都会更新三次。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So we're talking about timelines and how things are changing. So I've seen these stats that you've shared, other folks at Anthropic have shared about how much of your code is now written by AI. So people have shared stats from 70% to 90%. There was an engineer lead that shared 90% of your code roughly is written by AI now, which first of all is just insane that it went from zero to 90%, I don't know, a few years, something like that. Yeah, basically. I don't think people are talking about this enough. That's just wild. You guys are basically at the bleeding edge. I've never heard a company that has this high a percentage of code being written by AI. (00:12:34): So you guys are at the edge of where things are heading. I think most companies will get here. How has product development changed knowing so much of your code is now written by AI, so usually it's like PM, it's like here's what we're building, engineer builds it, it ships it. Is it still kind of roughly that or is it now PMs are just going straight to Claude, build this thing for me, engineers are doing different things? Just what looks different in a world where 90% of your code is written by AI?
turns.zh: 接下来我们要谈谈时间线以及事物如何演变。我看到你分享的这些数据，还有Anthropic的其他同事也提到，现在你们的代码有多少是由AI编写的。有人分享的数据显示比例从70%到90%不等。有一位工程主管称，现在你们大约90%的代码都是由AI编写的。首先，从零到90%，在短短几年内达到这个比例简直令人难以置信。是啊，这确实太惊人了。你们简直走在了技术前沿。我从未听说过有哪家公司的代码被AI编写的比例能如此之高。（00:12:34）所以你们正处于行业发展的最前沿。我认为大多数公司最终都会达到这一水平。既然现在你们大量代码由AI编写，产品开发流程又有何变化呢？传统流程通常是产品经理提出需求，工程师负责开发并上线。但现在情况是否有所不同？比如，产品经理是否直接对Claude下达任务，让它为自己构建产品？工程师们又在做哪些新的工作？在90%代码由AI编写的世界里，产品开发流程到底有何不同？

turns.speaker: Mike Krieger
turns.en: Yeah, it's really interesting because I think the role of engineering has changed a lot, but the suite of people that come together to produce a product hasn't yet. And I think for the worst in a lot of ways because I think we're still holding on some assumptions. So I think the roles are still fairly similar, although we'll now get in my favorite things that happen now are some nice PMs that have an idea that they want to express or designers that have an idea they want to express will use Claude and maybe even Artifacts to put together an actual functional demo. And that has been very, very helpful. No, no, this is what I mean that makes it tangible. That's probably the biggest role shift is prototyping happening earlier in the process via more of this code plus design piece. What I've learned though is the process of knowing what to ask the AI, how to compose the question, how to even think about structuring a change between the backend and the front end. (00:13:54): Those are still very difficult and specialized skills and they still require the engineer to think about it. And we really rapidly became bottlenecked on other things like our merge queue, which is the get in line to get your change accepted by the system that then deploys into production. We had to completely re-architect it because so much more code was being written and so many more pull requests were being submitted that it just completely blew out the expectations of it. And so it's like, I don't know if you've ever read, is it the goal, the classic process optimization book, and you realize there's this critical path theory. I've just found all these new bottlenecks in our system, there's an upstream bottleneck, which is decision making and alignment. A lot of things that I'm thinking about right now is how do I provide the minimum viable strategy to let people feel empowered to go run and type and build and explore at the edge of model capabilities. (00:14:44): I don't think I've gotten that right yet, but that's something I'm working on. And then once the building is happening, other bottlenecks emerge, let's make sure we don't step on each other's toes. Let's think through all the edge cases here ahead of time so that we're not blocked on the engineering side. And then when the work is complete and we're getting ready to ship it, what are all those bottlenecks as well? Let's do the air traffic control of landing the change. How do we figure out large strategy? So I think there hasn't been as much pressure on changing those until this year, but I would expect that a year from now the way that we are conceiving of building and shipping software just changes a lot because it's going to be very painful to do it the current way.
turns.zh: 是啊，这确实很有趣。我认为工程师的角色发生了巨大变化，但参与产品开发的团队协作模式却尚未跟上步伐。在某种程度上，这甚至可能带来负面影响，因为我们仍在固守一些过时的假设。因此，尽管工程师的角色仍大体相似，但如今我最喜欢看到的是一些优秀的产品经理（PM）能清晰表达自己的构想，或者设计师能将创意付诸实践。他们会借助Claude等工具，甚至Artifacts平台，快速搭建出可用的演示原型。这对我们帮助极大。不，不，这才是真正让问题具象化的关键所在。最大的角色转变或许在于，原型设计在开发流程中愈发重要，结合了更多代码与设计元素。我深有体会的是，如何向AI提出有效问题，如何构思问题结构，如何协调前后端的变更流程，这些都需要工程师亲自把关。我们很快在合并队列（merge queue）上遇到瓶颈——即代码合并到生产环境的排队机制。由于提交的代码量激增，合并请求数量爆增，导致系统超出预期负荷。我们不得不彻底重构整个流程。说到这，你或许读过《目标》（Goal）这本经典流程优化书籍，里面提到的关键路径理论让我深有共鸣。我在系统中发现了许多新瓶颈，比如上游的决策与协作瓶颈。目前我正致力于制定最小可行策略，让团队能在模型能力边界内自由探索、构建与迭代。虽然目前尚未完全掌握，但这是我正在努力的方向。等到开发阶段，新的瓶颈又接踵而至，比如避免各团队重复造轮子，提前预判所有边缘场景，避免工程层面受阻。最后，上线前又会面临一系列合并协调难题，如何统一大策略？直到今年，我们才真正感受到改变的紧迫性，但我相信一年后构建与上线软件的思路将彻底革新，因为现有模式的成本实在太高了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow, that is extremely interesting. So it used to be here's an idea, let's go design it, build it, ship it, merge it, and then ship it. And usually the bottleneck was engineering, taking time to build a thing and then design. And now you're saying the two bottlenecks you're finding are okay deciding what to build and aligning everyone and then it's actually the cue to merge it into production. And I imagine review it too is probably a part-
turns.zh: 哇，这真是太有意思了。过去的流程是先有想法，再设计，再开发，再合并，最后上线。而现在你提到遇到的两个瓶颈，一个是确定要构建什么内容，另一个是团队协作与对齐。最后才是合并到生产环境。我想评审环节可能也是个重要环节——

turns.speaker: Mike Krieger
turns.en: Reviewing has really changed too. And in many ways perhaps unsurprisingly the team that works in the most futuristic way is the Claude Code team because they're using Claude Code to build Claude Code in a very self-improving kind of way. And early on in that project, they would do very line by line pull request reviews in the way that you would for any other project. And they've just realized Claude is generally right and it's producing pull requests that are probably larger than most people are going to be able to review. So can you use a different Claude to review it and then do the human almost acceptance testing more than trying to review line by line. There's definitely pros and cons and so far it's gone well. But I could also imagine it going off the rails and then having a completely both unmaintainable or even understandable by Claude Code base that hasn't happened, but watching them change their review processes definitely has been interesting. (00:16:38): And yeah, the merge queue is one instance of the bottom bottleneck that forms down there, but there's other ones which is how do we make sure that we're still building something coherent and packaging it up into a moment that we can share with people and whether that's around a launch moment, whether that's about then enabling people to use this thing and talking about it, the classic things of building something useful for people and then making it known that you've built it and then learning from their feedback still exists. We've just made a portion of that whole process much more efficient.
turns.zh: 代码评审确实变了。在很多方面，毫不意外，Claude Code团队的工作方式最具未来感，因为他们正在用Claude Code来构建Claude Code，形成一种自我改进的良性循环。在项目早期，他们像评审其他项目一样进行逐行代码拉取请求评审。但后来他们发现Claude通常能提供更准确的代码，生成的拉取请求规模可能超出大多数人能处理的范围。于是他们开始让不同的Claude来进行评审，而人类只需进行最终的验收测试，而非逐行评审。这种方法有利有弊，目前进展顺利。但我也能想象它可能会失控，导致Claude Code代码库既难以维护又难以理解。不过看着他们不断调整评审流程确实很有趣。（00:16:38）：是的，合并队列是底层瓶颈的一个例子，但还有其他挑战，比如如何确保我们构建的东西连贯，并将其打包成可与他人分享的成果，无论是发布时机，还是让用户使用并讨论产品——这些经典的步骤仍然适用。我们只是让整个过程更高效了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I heard you describe this as you guys are patient zero for this way of working.
turns.zh: 我听你说，你们是这种工作方式的先行者。

turns.speaker: Mike Krieger
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that. Do you have a sense of what percentage of Claude Code is written by Claude Code?
turns.zh: 我喜欢这一点。你知道Claude Code中有多少是Claude Code写的吗？

turns.speaker: Mike Krieger
turns.en: At this point, I would be shocked if it wasn't 95% plus. I'd have to ask Boris and the other tech leads on there. But what's been cool is so nitty-gritty stuff, Claude Code is written in TypeScript. It's actually our largest TypeScript project. Most of the rest of Anthropic is written in Python, some Go, some Rust now, but we're not like a TypeScript shop. And so I saw a great comment yesterday in our Slack where somebody had this thing that was driving them crazy about Claude Code and they're like, "Well, I don't know any TypeScript, I'm just going to talk to Claude about it and do it." (00:17:49): And they went from that to pull requests in an hour and solve their problem and they submitted a pull request and that breaking down the barriers. One, it changes your barrier to entry for any kind of newcomer to the project. I think it can let you choose the right language for the right job for example. I think that helps as well, but I think it also just reinforces Claude Code being that patient alpha of that where contributions from outside the team can be Claude coded as well.
turns.zh: 目前，如果不是95%以上，我都会很惊讶。我得去问问Boris和其他技术负责人。但有趣的是，Claude Code是用TypeScript写的，这是我们最大的TypeScript项目。Anthropic的大部分其他代码用Python写，还有一些Go和Rust，但我们不是专注于TypeScript的团队。所以昨天我在Slack上看到一个很棒的评论，有人因为Claude Code的问题抓狂，他们说：“好吧，我不会TypeScript，我就去和Claude聊聊。”（00:17:49）：结果他们在一小时内就完成了拉取请求，解决了问题并提交了请求。这打破了障碍。一方面，它降低了新人加入项目的门槛。我认为它能让人们为合适的工作选择合适的语言，这也很有帮助，但我觉得它也强化了Claude Code作为先行者的地位，外部贡献者也能用Claude Code进行贡献。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow, this is, it's just continue to blow my mind all these things that you're sharing, 95% of Claude Code is written by Claude Code roughly.
turns.zh: 哇，所有你分享的这些东西都让我惊叹不已，Claude Code大约95%是Claude Code写的。

turns.speaker: Mike Krieger
turns.en: That's my guess. Yeah, I'll come back with the real stuff. But I mean if you ask the team, that's how they're working and that's how they're getting contributions from across the company too.
turns.zh: 这是我的猜测。是的，我会再去确认具体数据。但我的意思是，如果你问团队成员，他们就是这样工作的，也是这样从公司各部门获得贡献的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's interesting going back to your point about strategy being assisted by Claude itself and your point about how a lot of the bottlenecks now are kind of the top of the funnel of coming up with ideas aligning everyone, it's interesting that Claude is already helping with that also of helping you decide what to build. So if those two bottlenecks are aligning, deciding what to build and then just merging and getting everything, where do you see the most interesting stuff happening to help you speed those things up?
turns.zh: 回到你之前提到的策略是由Claude自身辅助的，以及目前很多瓶颈都集中在创意产生和团队协作这两个环节上。有趣的是，Claude已经在这些方面提供帮助，比如帮助你决定要开发什么产品。那么，如果这两个瓶颈能协同解决——确定要开发什么产品，然后整合资源——你认为最有价值的创新点会出现在哪里？如何加速这些进程？

turns.speaker: Mike Krieger
turns.en: Yeah, I think that on that first row, I started the year by writing a doc that was effectively how do we do product today and where is Claude not showing up yet that it should? And I think that upstream part is the next one to go. It's interesting. At your conference I talked to somebody who's working on a PRD, GPT kind of ChatPRD, I think was the-
turns.zh: 是的，我记得今年年初我写了一份文档，基本上是关于我们如何在当下进行产品开发，以及Claude在哪些方面尚未达到预期效果的。接下来要解决的难题是上游部分。这很值得期待。在你的会议上，我和一位正在开发PRD（产品路线图）的GPT聊天机器人的人聊过，我记得他提到的是ChatPRD，[00:19:24听不清]。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: ChatPRD, [inaudible 00:19:24].
turns.zh: ChatPRD，[00:19:24听不清]。

turns.speaker: Mike Krieger
turns.en: Yeah. Can Claude be a partner in figuring out what to build? What the market size is if you want to approach it that way? What the user needs are if you look at a different way? We think a lot about the virtual collaborator on topic and one of the ways in which I think that can show up is, "Hey, I'm in the Discord, the Claude Anthropic Discord, I'm in the user Fora, I'm on X and I'm reading things and here's what's emergent." That's step one. Models can do that today. Step two, which the models probably can do today, which have to wire them up to do it is and not only are the problems here's how I think you might be able to solve them. And then taking that through to, and I put together a pull request to solve this thing that I'm seeing feels very achievable this year than stringing those things together and we're limited more. (00:20:13): This is why MCP is exciting to me. We're limited more around making sure the context flows through all of that so we have the right access to those things more than the model's capability to reason and propose. Now the model might not have perfect UI taste yet, so there's definitely room for design to intervene and be like, "Oh, that's not quite how I would solve the problem of this not showing up." But I would get very excited. I would give you a really small example, but we changed on Claude AI, you should be able to just copy markdown from Artifacts or code from Artifacts and we changed it so you can actually download it and export it. We changed the button to export and we got a bunch of feedback like, "How do I copy now?" And the answer is you drop it down and it's copied. (00:20:51): It's just mind one of those things where it's made sense, but we probably got it not quite right. That feedback was in the RUX channel. I would've loved an hour later for a plot to be like, "Hey, if we do want to change it back, here's the PR to do it." And by the way, eventually, and then I'm going to spin up an A/B test to see if this changes metrics and then we'll see how it looks in a week. If you told me that about a year and a half ago going to be like, "Ah, yeah, maybe like 27, maybe 26." But it really feels just at the tip of capabilities right now.
turns.zh: 是的。Claude能否成为确定产品方向的合作伙伴？如果想从市场规模入手，它能提供哪些洞察？如果从用户需求出发，又能提供哪些见解？我们一直在思考虚拟协作者这一概念，其中一个可能的应用场景是：“嘿，我在Claude的人工智能Discord群里，我在用户论坛上，我在X平台上看到一些内容，这里有一些新兴的需求。”这就是第一步。模型现在已经能做到这一点。第二步，模型或许也能实现，但需要接入相关系统。比如，当我发现某个问题时，可能需要提交一个pull request来解决。今年我认为把这些环节串联起来比以前更容易了。（00:20:13）这就是MCP（多模态交互平台）让我兴奋的地方。我们在确保上下文贯通方面还有很多改进空间，比如让模型不仅能识别问题，还能给出解决方案。目前模型可能还没有完美的UI设计感，所以设计团队可以介入，比如：“哦，这样处理问题可能更合适。”但我对此很期待。我举个小例子，我们改进了Claude AI的功能，现在你可以直接从Artifacts复制Markdown或代码，并下载导出。按钮改成了导出按钮，用户反馈说：“现在怎么复制？”答案是拖放即可。（00:20:51）这就是典型的改进案例，之前没做好，现在改进了。反馈来自RUX频道。要是当时能在一小时后快速做一个A/B测试，告诉大家如果想改回去，PR已经提交了，那就太好了。顺便说一句，最终我们会做A/B测试，看看是否能提升指标，一周后再评估效果。如果一年半前有人跟我说这些，我可能会说：“嗯，可能27分左右，26分吧。”但现在感觉这些功能真的即将触达极限了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow, okay. You mentioned the Lenny and Friends Summit. I wanted to talk about this a bit. So you were on a panel with Kevin Weil, the CPO of OpenAI, I think it was the first time you guys did this maybe the last time for now.
turns.zh: 哇，好的。你提到了Lenny and Friends峰会。我想稍微聊聊这个。当时你和OpenAI的CPO凯文·韦尔同台讨论，我记得这是你们第一次合作，可能也是暂时最后一次。

turns.speaker: Mike Krieger
turns.en: Yeah, we haven't done it since, not for any reason. I had a lot of fun.
turns.zh: 是啊，从那以后我们就再没这么做过了，但不是因为别的原因。我玩得很开心。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What a legendary panel we assembled there with Sarah Guo moderating. And you made this comment actually ended up being the most rewatched part of the interview, which is that you were putting product people on the model team and working with researchers making the model better and you're putting some product people on the product experience making the UX more intuitive, making all that better. And you found that almost all the leverage came from the product team working with the researchers. And so you've been doing more of that. So first of all, does that continue to be true? And second of all, what are the implications of that for product teams?
turns.zh: 我们在那里组建的那个小组真是太棒了，由郭莎莎担任主持人。你提到的那个评论最终成了采访中观看次数最多的部分——你提到让产品人员加入模型团队，与研究人员合作优化模型，同时让一些产品人员参与产品体验设计，提升用户体验。结果发现，大部分的成效都来自产品团队与研究人员的深度协作。所以你一直在加强这种合作。首先，这种模式是否依然有效？其次，这对产品团队意味着什么？

turns.speaker: Mike Krieger
turns.en: It's continued to be true. And in fact I think that if the proportion was already skewing towards having more of that embedding, I've just become more and more convinced. I didn't feel as strongly about it during the summit and now I feel really strongly about it. If we're shipping things that could have been built by anybody just using our models off the shelf, there's great stuff to be built by using our models off the shelf by the way, don't get me wrong, but where we should play and what we can do uniquely should be stuff that's really at that magic intersection between the two, right? (00:22:42): Artifacts may a great example and if you play with Artifacts with Claude 4, that's an actually really interesting example where we took somebody from our, we have Claude code skills, which is a team that really is doing the post-training around teaching Claude some of these really specific skills and we paired it with some product people and then together we revamped how this looks in the product today and what Claude can do way better than just like, "Yeah, we just used the model and we prompted a little bit." (00:23:07): That's just not enough. We need to be in that fine-tuning process. So much of what, if you look at what we're working on right now, but we've shipped recently between research and all these other things are things that the functional unit of work at Anthropic is no longer take the model and then go work with design and product to go ship a product. It's more like we are in the post-training conversations around how these things should work and then we are in the building process and we're feeding those things back and looping them back. (00:23:36): I think it's exciting. It's also a new way of working that not all PMs have, but the PMs that have the most internal positive feedback from both research and engineering are the ones that get it that I was in a product review yesterday, I was like, "Oh, if we want to do this memory feature, we should talk to the researchers because we just shipped a bunch of memory capabilities in Claude 4." They're like, "Yeah, yeah, we've been talking to them for weeks, this is how we're manifesting it." It's like, "Okay, I feel good. I feel like we're doing the right things now."
turns.zh: 这种模式确实有效。事实上，我认为如果这种嵌入式合作的比例已经在上升，那我对它的信心就更加坚定了。在峰会期间我对此还不是很确定，但现在我深信不疑。如果我们推出的产品只是用现成的模型就能开发的，那当然很棒——别误会我的意思，但我们应该专注于在模型与用户体验之间找到那个神奇的交集，对吧？（00:22:42）：Artifacts 就是一个很好的例子。如果你用 Claude 4 和 Artifacts 一起操作，那就是一个非常有趣的案例。我们让 Claude 代码团队（一个专门负责训练后优化、教授 Claude 特定技能的团队）与产品团队合作，共同优化了现有产品的界面，让 Claude 的能力远不止于“用模型加点提示语”那么简单。（00:23:07）：这还远远不够。我们需要深入调优流程。看看我们现在正在做的项目，以及近期从研究部门推出的成果，就会发现 Anthropic 的产品开发模式不再是简单地把模型交给设计和产品团队去开发产品。现在更多的是在训练后阶段共同探讨产品应该如何运作，然后再投入开发，形成闭环反馈。（00:23:36）：我觉得这很令人兴奋。这也是一种新的工作方式，虽然不是所有产品经理都掌握，但那些能从研究和工程团队获得积极反馈的产品经理，都能理解其中的价值。昨天我在参加产品评审会时，他们提到要开发某项内存功能，我说应该和研究团队沟通，因为我们刚在 Claude 4 中加入了一堆内存相关功能。他们回答：“是啊，我们已经和他们沟通几周了，这就是我们要实现的方案。”我当时就觉得很欣慰，感觉我们现在做得很对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So let me pull on this thread more and there's something I've been thinking about along these lines. So essentially there's a big part of entropic that's building this super intelligent giga brain that's going to do all these things for us over time. And then, as you said, there's the product team that's building the UX around this super intelligent giga brain and over time this super intelligence is going to be able to build its own stuff. And so I guess just where do you think the most value will come from traditional product teams over time? I know this is different because you guys are a foundational alum company and not most companies don't work this way, but just, I don't know, thoughts on just the where most value will come from product teams over time working on AI.
turns.zh: 接下来，我想再深入探讨一下这个话题。说到这里，我一直在思考一个关键问题：在未来，Entropic公司将打造一个超级智能的巨型大脑，逐渐为我们完成各种任务。正如你所说，产品团队需要围绕这个超级智能大脑设计用户体验，而随着时间推移，这个超级智能系统还将能够自主研发产品。那么，你认为传统产品团队未来最能创造价值的领域在哪里？我知道你们Entropic是创始人主导的公司，多数公司并非如此运作，但我还是想谈谈在人工智能时代，产品团队的价值所在。

turns.speaker: Mike Krieger
turns.en: I think there's still a lot of value in two things. One is making this all comprehensible. I think we've done an okay job. I think we could do a much better job of making this conference. What's still the difference between somebody who's really adept at using these tools in their work and most people is huge. And maybe that's the most literal answer to your earlier question around what skills to learn. That is a skill to learn and use it in the same way that I remember we did computer lock class when I was in middle school. I remember being really good at Google and that was actually a skill back in the day to think in terms of this information is out there, how do I query for it? How do I do it? I think it actually was an advantage at the time. (00:25:21): Of course now Google is pretty good at figuring out what you're trying to do if you are only in the neighborhood and there's less of that research kind of need. But I still think that's a necessary part of good product development, which is the capabilities are there and even if Claude can create products from scratch, what are you building and how do you make it Comprehensible? Still hard because I think that gets at this much deeper empathy and understanding of human needs and psychology. I was a human community interaction major, I still been talking in my book here. I still feel like that is a very, very, very, very necessary skill. So that's one. Two is, and this straight to call back to another one of your guests, strategy, how we win, where we'll play, figuring out where exactly you're going to want to, of all the things that you could be spending your time or your tokens or your computation on what you want to actually go and do. (00:26:15): You could be wider probably than you could before, but you can't do everything. And even from an external perspective, if you're seen to be doing everything, it's way less clear around how you're positioning yourselves. Like strategy I think is still the second piece. And then the third one is opening people's eyes to what's possible, which is a continuation of making it understandable. But we were in a demo with a financial services company recently and we were working on here's how you can use our analysis tool and MCP together and you could see their light up and you're like, "Ah, okay." We call it overhang. The delta between what the models and the products can do and how they're being used on a daily basis. Huge overhang. So that's where still a very, very strong necessary role for product.
turns.zh:
我认为仍有两个方面蕴藏着巨大价值。首先是让整个系统易于理解。我觉得我们在这方面做得还不错，但仍有很大的提升空间。比如在本次大会上，对于那些真正善于运用这些工具的人和普通用户之间的差距，仍然巨大。这或许就是你之前提到的学习技能的最直白答案——学会如何使用这些工具，就像我中学时学的计算机锁课一样。当时我记得自己很擅长谷歌搜索，这在当时就是一项宝贵技能：如何高效获取信息？如何快速实现目标？这在当时确实是一种优势。（00:25:21）当然现在谷歌已经能很准确地理解你的需求，但这种研究型思维的需求正在减少。但我仍然认为，这是产品开发的核心要素——即便Claude能从零开始打造产品，但你要构建什么？如何让产品易于理解？这依然是个挑战，因为这需要深刻理解人类需求和心理。我曾主修人类社区互动专业，这在我的书中也有提及。我仍然认为这是一项极其重要的技能。

第二点是战略规划，即如何取胜、选择战场、明确优先级。在众多可投入时间、资源和算力的方向中，如何精准聚焦核心任务？（00:26:15）你可能比过去拥有更广阔的视野，但无法面面俱到。即使从外部视角看，你若显得无所不能，反而会让定位模糊。比如战略规划仍是关键环节。第三点是让人们看到可能性边界的拓展，这也是易于理解的延续。比如我们最近与一家金融服务公司合作，展示如何将分析工具与MCP协同使用，看到他们眼中焕发光彩时，你会感叹“原来如此！”。我们称之为“认知鸿沟”——模型与产品实际应用之间的巨大落差。这正是产品团队不可或缺的价值所在。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, that's an awesome answer. So essentially areas for product teams to lean into more is strategy, just getting better and better at strategy, figuring out what to build and how to win in the market, making it easier to help people understand how to leverage the power of these tools, the comprehensibility and kind of along those lines is opening people's eyes to the potential of these sorts of things. That's where product can still help.
turns.zh: 好的，这是一个很棒的回答。基本上，产品团队可以深挖的领域在于策略——不断提升策略能力、明确该开发什么产品以及如何在市场中取胜。让人们更容易理解如何利用这些工具的强大功能，提升其可理解性——这类举措能让人们意识到这类技术的潜力。这正是产品部门仍能发挥作用的地方。

turns.speaker: Mike Krieger
turns.en: Exactly.
turns.zh: 没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. So along those lines actually, do you have any just prompting tricks for people, things that you've learned to get more out of Claude when you chat with it?
turns.zh: 太棒了。说到这，你有没有什么提示技巧可以分享？比如在与Claude聊天时，怎样才能更好地利用它？

turns.speaker: Mike Krieger
turns.en: Sometimes it's funny because in some ways we have the ultimate prompting job, which is to write the system prompt for Claudia AI and we publish all of these, which I think is another nice area of transparency. And we are always careful when giving prompting advice because at least officially, but I'll give you the unofficial version because you don't want things to become like we think this works, but we're not sure why. But I will do small things like in Claude Code and we actually do react to this very literally, but I always ask it to, if I wanted to use more reasoning, think hard and it'll use a different flow and I usually start with that. Nudging, there's a great essay around make the other mistake like if you tend to be too nice, can you focus on... Even if you're trying to be more critical or more blunt, you're probably not going to be the most critical blunt person in the world. (00:28:18): And so with Claude sometimes I'm like, "Be brutal, Claude, roast me. Tell me what's wrong with this strategy." I know we were talking earlier about the Claude as thought partner around critiquing product strategy. I think I previously would say things like, "What could be better on this product strategy?" And I'm just like, "Just roast this product strategy," and Claude's like a pretty nice entity. It's hard to push it to be super brutal, but it forces it to be a little bit more critical as well. The last thing I'll say is, so we have a team called Applied AI that does a lot of work with our customers around optimizing Claude for their use case. And we basically took their insights and their way of working and we put it into a product itself. So if you go to our console, our work bench, we have this thing called the prompt improver where you describe the problem and you give it examples and Claude itself will agentically create and then iterate on a prompt for you. (00:29:09): I find what comes out of that ends up being quite different than what my intuitions would've been for a good prompt. And so I'd encourage folks to also check that out even for their own use cases because while that tool is met for an API developer putting a prompt into their product, it's equally applicable for a person doing a prompt for themselves. It'll insert XML tags which no human is going to think to do ahead of time. It actually is very helpful for Claude to understand what it should be thinking versus what it should be saying, et cetera. So that's another one is watch our prompt improver and then note that Claude itself is a very good prompter of Claude.
turns.zh: 有时候挺有趣的，因为某种程度上，我们承担着终极提示任务——为Claudia AI编写系统提示语，并公开所有这些提示语，我认为这也是透明度的一个亮点。不过在提供提示建议时，我们总是很谨慎，至少在官方层面是这样。但我可以分享一些非官方的经验，因为你肯定不希望人们觉得“我们觉得这个方法有效，但自己也不太清楚原因”。比如在Claude Code里，我们会非常字面地处理用户的需求，但我通常会要求它如果想用更多推理逻辑，就得仔细思考。这通常是我的起点。还有关于“犯别人的错误”的理念，比如如果你太善良，别人可能会利用这一点。（00:28:18）有时我会对Claude说：“残忍点吧，Claude，批评我吧。告诉我这个策略有什么问题。” 我们之前讨论过Claude作为思维伙伴在批评产品策略方面的作用。以前我可能会问“这个产品策略还能怎么优化？” 但现在我会直接说：“直接批评这个产品策略。” 而Claude其实是个相当友好的实体。很难逼它变得特别严厉，但这确实能促使它更具批判性。最后我想说，我们有一个名为Applied AI的团队，他们与客户密切合作，优化Claude以适应他们的使用场景。我们基本上收集了他们的见解和工作方式，并将其转化为产品本身。所以如果你访问我们的控制台或工作台，我们有一个叫做“提示改进器”的功能。你描述问题，提供示例，Claude会主动为你创建并迭代提示语。（00:29:09）我发现最终得到的结果与我自己对优秀提示语的直觉大不相同。因此，我鼓励大家也试试这个工具，哪怕只是为了自己的使用场景。虽然这个工具主要面向将提示语集成到产品中的API开发者，但它同样适用于为自己创建提示语的人。 它会插入XML标签，人类通常不会提前想到这些。实际上，这对Claude理解应该思考什么而不是说什么非常有帮助。所以另一个建议是，试试我们的提示改进器，然后注意Claude本身也是一个非常优秀的提示生成器。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Okay, so we're going to link to that, the prompt improver. The core piece of advice you shared early is just do the opposite of what you would naturally do. So if you're trying to be nice, just be brutal, be very honest and frank with me.
turns.zh: 太棒了。好的，我们要链接到那个提示改进工具。你早前分享的核心建议就是做与直觉相反的事。所以如果你想表现得友善，那就 brutal 一点，对我要非常诚实和坦率。

turns.speaker: Mike Krieger
turns.en: Exactly. I find that works quite well. What are the thought patterns that I've fallen into that you want to break me out of?
turns.zh: 没错。我发现这方法效果很好。你想让我改掉哪些思维定式呢？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I saw you guys just today maybe launched a Rick Rubin collab where it said vibe coding. What's that all about?
turns.zh: 我今天刚看到你们可能推出了与里克·鲁宾的合作项目，叫做“氛围编码”。这到底是什么意思？

turns.speaker: Mike Krieger
turns.en: What I've heard about that. And again, a lot of the coalesce this week between model launch developer event and The Way of Code. We had one of our co-founders, Jack Clark is our head of policy and he got connected to Rick Rubin because I think he's been thinking a lot about coding, the future of coding and creativity and they've stayed in touch. And Rick got excited about this idea of he was creating art and visualizations with Claude and then he had these ideas around the way of the vibe coder and they put together this, actually I mean I love almost everything Rick Rubin. So the aesthetic of it I think is just so on point too. But yeah, this sort of like med meditation is probably the right word. Meditation on creativity, working alongside AI coupled with this really rich, interesting visualizations. But it's one of those things where internally they're like, "Oh yeah, and we're doing this Rick Rubin collab." We were like, "We're doing what? That's amazing."
turns.zh: 我听说过相关消息。这周“模型发布开发者活动”和“编程之道”两者融合得非常紧密。我们公司的联合创始人杰克·克拉克是政策主管，他与里克·鲁宾结缘，因为里克一直在思考编程、编程的未来和创造力等问题，他们一直保持着联系。里克对用 Claude 创作艺术和可视化作品很感兴趣，然后又有了“氛围编码者”的概念，他们共同打造了这个项目。说实话，我几乎喜欢里克·鲁宾的一切作品。他的美学理念也太到位了。但这确实有点像冥想——是对创造力的沉思，与人工智能协同工作，再加上这些丰富有趣的可视化效果。不过内部团队一开始听到“要和里克·鲁宾合作”时，都惊呼：“哦，什么鬼？太棒了！”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I looked at it briefly and there's that meme of him just thinking deeply, sitting on a computer with a mouth.
turns.zh: 我简单看了一下，里面有个他深思熟虑、坐在电脑前、嘴巴张着的梗图。

turns.speaker: Mike Krieger
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 对啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And ASCII art, I think.
turns.zh: 还有 ASCII 艺术，我觉得。

turns.speaker: Mike Krieger
turns.en: It's totally, it's like ASCII art vibe.
turns.zh: 完全是 ASCII 艺术的氛围。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm excited to have Andrew Luo joining us today. Andrew is CEO of OneSchema, one of our long time podcast sponsors. Welcome, Andrew.
turns.zh: 很高兴今天安德鲁·罗能加入我们。安德鲁是 OneSchema 的首席执行官，也是我们长期的播客赞助商之一。欢迎你，安德鲁。

turns.speaker: Speaker 3
turns.en: Thanks for having me, Lenny. Great to be here.
turns.zh: 感谢邀请，莱尼。很高兴能来。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So what is new with one schema? I know that you work with some of my favorite companies like Ramp and Vanta and Watershed. I heard you guys launch a new data intake product that automates the hours of manual work that teams spent importing and mapping and integrating CSV and Excel files.
turns.zh: 那么 OneSchema 有哪些新动态？我知道你与 Ramp、Vanta 和 Watershed 等我最喜欢的公司合作。我听说你们推出了一个新的数据导入产品，可以自动化处理团队在导入、映射和整合 CSV 及 Excel 文件时耗费的大量手动工作。

turns.speaker: Speaker 3
turns.en: Yes, so we just launched the 2.0 of OneSchema FileFeeds. We've rebuilt it from the ground up with AI. We saw so many customers coming to us with teams of data engineers that struggled with the manual work required to clean messy spreadsheets. FileFeeds 2.0 allows non-technical teams to automate the process of transforming CSV and Excel files with just a simple prompt. We support all of the trickiest file integrations, SFTP, S3, and even email.
turns.zh: 是的，我们刚刚推出了 OneSchema FileFeeds 2.0。我们完全从头开始用 AI 重建了它。我们发现很多客户带着数据工程师团队来找我们，他们在清理混乱的电子表格时遇到了困难。FileFeeds 2.0 让非技术团队只需一个简单的提示，就能自动化处理 CSV 和 Excel 文件的转换过程。我们支持所有最棘手的文件集成，比如 SFTP、S3 甚至电子邮件。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I can tell you that if my team had to build integrations like this, how nice would it be to take this off our roadmap and instead use something like OneSchema?
turns.zh: 我可以想象，如果我的团队要开发这样的集成功能，能把这部分从路线图中移除，转而使用 OneSchema 会多好啊？

turns.speaker: Speaker 3
turns.en: Absolutely, Lenny. We've heard so many horror stories of outages from even just a single bad record in transactions, employee files, purchase orders, you name it. Debugging these issues is often like finding a needle in a haystack. OneSchema stops any bad data from entering your system and automatically validates your files, generating error reports with the exact issues in all bad files.
turns.zh: 确实如此，莱尼。我们听过太多因为交易记录、员工档案、采购订单等单个数据错误导致系统崩溃的恐怖故事。调试这些问题往往就像大海捞针一样困难。OneSchema 能有效阻止错误数据进入系统，还能自动验证文件，并生成包含所有错误文件精确问题的错误报告。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I know that importing incorrect data can cause all kinds of pain for your customers and quickly lose their trust. Andrew, thank you so much for joining me. If you want to learn more, head on over to oneschema.co. That's oneschema.co. (00:32:48): Actually going back to the beginning of your journey at Anthropic, what's the story of you getting recruited at Anthropic? Is there anything fun there?
turns.zh: 我知道导入错误数据会给客户带来诸多困扰，甚至迅速丧失他们的信任。安德鲁，非常感谢你参与我们的访谈。如果你想了解更多信息，可以访问 oneschema.co 网站。（00:32:48）：说回你在 Anthropic 的职业生涯初期，你是如何被招入 Anthropic 的？这段经历有什么趣事吗？

turns.speaker: Mike Krieger
turns.en: It all started and I actually sent my friend this text. So Joel Lewenstein, who I've known, he and I built our first iPhone apps together in 2007 when the App Store was just out and you could still make money by selling dollar apps on the App Store back in the day. And we were both at Stanford together and we were friends and we've stayed in touch over years and we've never gotten to work together since then. We've just remained close. And I was coming out of the Artifact experience, I was trying to figure out, do I start another company? I don't think so. I need a break from starting something from zero. Do I go work somewhere? I don't know what company would I want to go work at. And he reached out and he's like, "Look, I don't know if you at all considered joining something rather than starting something, but we're looking for a CPO. Would you be interested in chatting?" (00:33:37): And at that time, Claude 3 had just come out and I was like, "Okay, this company's clearly got a good research team. The product is so early still." And it was like, "Great, I'll take the meeting." And I first met with Daniela, was one of the co-founders and the president in Anthropic. And just from the beginning I was like a breath of fresh air, very little grandiosity coming off the founders, I mean they're clear-eyed about what they're building. They know what they don't know. How many times I talk to Dario always like Dario is like, "Look, I don't know anything about product, but here's an intuition." Usually the intuition is really good and leads to some good conversation, but I think that intellectual honesty and shared view of what it means to do AI in a responsible way, it just resonated. (00:34:22): I kept having this feeling in these interviews, this is the AI company I would've hoped to have found it if I had founded an AI company. And that's kind of the bar around if I'm going to join something that should be where I'm going to go. But what I realized, I actually hadn't joined a company since my first internship in college basically. And I was like, "Oh, how do I onboard myself? How do I get myself up to speed? How do I balance making sweeping changes versus understanding what's not broken about it overall?" And looking back on a year, I think I made some changes too slowly. I think there was ways reorganizing product that I could have made a change earlier. And I think I didn't appreciate how much a couple of really key senior people can shape so much of product strategy. (00:35:10): I'll harken back to Claude Code. Claude Code happened because Boris, who actually was a Boris Cherney, he was an Instagram engineer and one of our senior ICs there, we overlapped a bit, was started that project from scratch internal first and then we got it out and then shipped it. And that's the power of one or two really strong people. And I made this mistake, we need more headcount and we do, I think there's more work that we need to do and there's things that I want to be building. But more than that we need a couple of almost founder type engineers that maybe connect back to our question on what skills are useful and how does product development change. And maybe even more so I'm a huge believer in the founding engineer tech lead with an idea and pair them with the right design and product supports, help them realize that, I'm 10 times more a believer in that than before.
turns.zh:
这一切始于我给朋友发了一条短信。乔尔·勒文斯坦（Joel Lewenstein）是我认识的人，我们在2007年一起开发了首款iPhone应用，当时App Store刚刚上线，通过在App Store上销售1美元应用还能赚到钱。我们曾在斯坦福大学同窗，后来保持联系，但一直没有再合作过。最近我刚结束在Artifact的创业经历，正犹豫是否要创办新公司，但又觉得自己需要休息一下。乔尔突然联系我，说：“你有没有考虑过加入一家公司而非自己创业？我们正在寻找首席产品官，你有兴趣聊聊吗？”（00:33:37）

当时Claude 3刚推出，我心想：“这家公司显然有很棒的研发团队，但产品还处于早期阶段。”于是我决定参加面试。首先见到了Anthropic的联合创始人兼总裁丹妮拉（Daniela）。这位创始人给人耳目一新的感觉，既不自负又脚踏实地，他们清楚自己的局限。达里奥（Dario）常说：“我对产品一窍不通，但我有个直觉。”这些直觉往往很准确，引发热烈讨论。最让我共鸣的是，他们对负责任地开展AI研究的共同理念。

（00:34:22）在面试中，我总有种感觉：这就是我理想中的AI公司，如果自己创办的话，希望能成为这样的团队。以此为标准衡量加入的公司才最合适。但我意识到，自大学实习结束后，自己就再没加入过新公司。我问自己：“如何快速融入？如何快速上手？如何平衡大刀阔斧的改革与充分理解现有框架？”回首过去一年，我觉得自己变革太慢了。比如产品重组本可以更早推进，而一些关键高管对产品战略的影响力之大让我深有体会。

（00:35:10）回想Claude Code项目，之所以能成功，是因为Instagram工程师、我们的资深IC之一鲍里斯·切尔尼（Boris Cherney）从零开始内部开发，再推向市场。这显示了少数核心人才的强大力量。我犯了错误，认为需要更多人手，但更需要几位创始人级别的工程师来重塑产品战略。或许更重要的是，我坚信创始人型工程师主导产品开发，搭配合适的设计和产品支持团队的模式。我对这种模式的信念比以往更坚定了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I actually asked people on Twitter what to ask you ahead of this conversation. And the most common question surprisingly was why did you shut down Artifact? And I also wondered that because I loved Artifact. I was a power user. I was just like, "Finally a news app that I love that it's giving me what I want to know." So I guess just what happened there at the end?
turns.zh: 实际上，在这次对话开始前，我在推特上问过大家应该问你些什么问题。结果最常见的问题居然是，你为什么关闭了Artifact？我也对此感到困惑，因为我特别喜欢Artifact。我曾是它的超级用户，当时特别兴奋地想：“终于有了一款我喜欢的资讯应用，它能给我推送我想了解的信息。”所以我想知道，最后到底发生了什么？

turns.speaker: Mike Krieger
turns.en: I still really miss it too. I didn't find a replacement and I think I substituted it by visiting individual sites and keeping things up that way. And it's not really the same, especially on the log to I think we got right with Artifact and if people didn't play with it before, it was we really tried to not just recommend top stories, they were part of it. But really if you were interested in Japanese architecture, you could pretty reliably get really interesting stories about Japanese architecture every day. Whether that's from a Dwell or from Architectural Digest or from a really specific blog that we found that somebody recommended to us. It captured some of that Google reader joy of content discovery of the deeper web. Our headwinds were a couple. One of them was just mobile websites have really taken a turn. I don't blame any individuals for this. (00:37:10): I think it's the market dynamics of it, but we put so much time or designers, sky Gunner Gray who's phenomenal that for Perplexity now, the app experience I was so proud of, but when you click through it was like the pressures on these mobile sites and these mobile publishers would be like, "Sign up for our newsletter. Here's a full screen video ad." It was very jarring and we didn't feel like it ethically made sense for us to do a bunch of ad blocking because then you're like, "Sure, you can deliver a nice experience for people, but that doesn't feel like it's playing fair with the publishers." But at the same time, the actual experience wasn't good. So the mobile web deteriorating, which makes me very sad, but I think was part of it. Two was Instagram spread in the early days because people would take photos and then post them on other networks and tell friends about it. (00:37:57): And there was this really natural like, "How did you do that? I want to do it." News was very personal. I can't tell you how many people would be like, "I love Artifact." I'm like, "Did you tell anybody about it?" And they're like, "I told one person," and it didn't have that kind of spread. And any attempt that we had to do it felt kind of contrived, like, "Oh, we'll wrap all the links in artifact.news." But we didn't want interstitial things. In some ways, this sounds very puritanical, I don't mean it to sound this way, but there were lines that we didn't want to cross that just felt ethically not us, that I've seen other news players do more of. And maybe if we had done that, it would've grown more, but I don't think that's the company we wanted to have built other way. I don't think we were the founders to have built it. (00:38:39): And the third one, which is an underappreciated one, is we started at mid-COVID, which meant that we were fully distributed and I think there were major shifts that we would've wanted to make both in the strategy and the product and the team. And it's really hard to do that if you are all fully remote. Nothing replaces the Instagram days of we went through some hard times like Ben Horowitz called the we're F'ed, it's over kind of moments. This is definitely type two fun. I wouldn't say that my favorite memories because they weren't happy ones, but memories I really stayed with me with Instagram was like me and Kevin at Taqueria, Cancun on Market Street eating burritos at literally 11:00 PM being like, "How are we going to get out of this? How are we going to work through this?" And Zoom is not a good replica for that. (00:39:26): You tend to let things go or things build up over time. So the confluence of those three things, we entered I guess 2024 and said, "Look, there is a company to be built in the space. I'm not sure where the people would've built it. This concurrent incarnation we love, but it's not growing." The way I put it's like 10 units of input in for one unit of output versus the other way around. If we put blood and tears into the product and launch something we were proud of and metrics would barely move, the energy is not present in this product, in this system. And so are we going to expend another year or two and then go off and fundraise only to find that this is the case or do we call it and see that it's run its course and try to find a home for it, et cetera. (00:40:06): So that was the confluence on it and they started feeling this opportunity cost of AI is starting to change everything. We have an AI powered news app, but is this the maximal way in which we're going to be able to impact this? And it felt like the answer was increasingly no. But it was hard. I mean in the end I was really at peace of the decision, but it was a conversation that went on for a couple of months.
turns.zh:
我现在还是很怀念它。我一直没找到合适的替代品，最后只能通过访问各个网站来维持更新，但效果完全不一样。尤其是订阅源方面，我觉得我们在Artifact上做得很成功——如果人们之前没用过这个功能，我们就努力不只是推荐头条新闻，而是让用户深度参与其中。比如，如果你对日本建筑感兴趣，每天都能看到有趣的相关内容，无论是来自Dwell、Architectural Digest，还是某个我们推荐的博客。这捕捉到了Google Reader那种探索深层网络内容的乐趣。我们的挑战主要有两个。一是移动网站的变革。我不怪任何人，只是市场动态使然。但我们投入了大量精力——比如设计师Sky Gunner Gray，他为Perplexity设计的应用体验让我深感自豪——但当用户点击链接时，却会被推送订阅提示和全屏广告。这让人很不适，同时我们也不想用广告拦截器，因为这感觉对发布商不公平。但实际体验太差了。移动网络的衰退让我很痛心，但这确实是部分原因。二是Instagram早期的发展。用户拍照后会上传到其他平台并分享给朋友。新闻本应是个性化的。我曾遇到很多人说"我超爱Artifact"，但当我问"你告诉过别人吗？"对方回答"只告诉过一个人"，传播效果就大打折扣。我们的推广尝试显得很生硬，比如用artifact.news包装所有链接，但我们不想加入强制广告。这听起来很道德化，但我们不想跨越某些底线——比如插入广告拦截器。这虽然能增加用户量，但不符合我们的价值观。（00:38:39）第三个被低估的挑战是我们在新冠疫情中期启动项目。这意味着完全远程办公，而我们本想在战略、产品和团队层面做出重大调整。但远程办公很难实现这些变革。没有什么能替代Instagram时代的集体奋斗——比如本·霍洛维茨说"我们完蛋了"的时刻。这绝对是第二类乐趣。虽然不是最美好的回忆，但Instagram让我难忘的时刻是凌晨11点和凯文在市场街的Taqueria Cancun吃卷饼，讨论如何摆脱困境。Zoom根本无法复现那种氛围。（00:39:26）问题是，要么放任问题发展，要么让问题积压。三者交汇之际，我们进入2024年，感叹道：
看哪，空间里要建一家公司了。我不确定人们原本会把它建在哪里。我们深爱这种并行发展模式，但它始终停滞不前。就拿我举例来说，投入十份精力却只能产出一份成果。若我们为产品倾注心血与汗水，推出令自己自豪的产品，却发现数据增长微乎其微，那么这款产品、这个系统本身就缺乏生命力。这意味着我们是应该再投入一两年时间，最终融资失败，还是应该及时止损，承认项目已走到尽头，为它另觅归宿？（00:40:06）这正是转折点——他们开始意识到，AI带来的机遇成本正在彻底改变一切。我们开发了AI驱动的新闻应用，但这是否就是我们能对行业产生最大影响的方式？答案似乎越来越否定。但这很难。说到底，我对这个决定心安理得，但这场讨论持续了好几个月。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: On that note, just how hard was it because because there's an ego component to it, like, "Oh, I'm starting my new company, it's going to be great," and then you end up having to shut it down. Just how hard is that as a very successful previous founder shutting something down and then not working out?
turns.zh: 就此而言，这确实挺难的，因为这里面有自负的成分，比如你会想：“哦，我要创办新公司了，肯定会大获成功。”结果最后却不得不关门大吉。作为一位成功的创业者，要关停一个项目却又未能成功，这得有多难？

turns.speaker: Mike Krieger
turns.en: Yeah, I mean I think when we started it, one of the conversations was like, "Look, what is the bar to success here? And do we want it to be something other than Instagram DAU?" Which is just an impossible bar. Only one company since, maybe two, you could say maybe ChatGPT and TikToK have reached that kind of mass consumer adoption starting a news app. Most people are not daily news readers even, right? And so we knew that we weren't pursuing that size of usage, at least with the first incarnation, but we did have an idea of building out complementary products over time that all use personalization and machine learning. We didn't even call it AI at the time. It was 2021 back-
turns.zh: 是啊，我觉得我们刚开始做这个项目时，讨论过一个问题：“看看，这里成功的标准是什么？我们是不是想让它超越Instagram的日活用户数？”但这实在是个不可能达到的标准。自那以后，或许只有两家公司——ChatGPT和TikTok——在用户基础上达到了这种级别的大规模普及。大多数人甚至都不是每日新闻读者，对吧？所以我们知道自己追求的用户规模不大——至少在最初的版本中是这样。但我们确实有想法，计划逐步开发更多互补产品，全部基于个性化和机器学习技术。当时我们甚至没用“人工智能”这个词，那还是2021年的事了——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, yeah, AI, it was called machine learning back then.
turns.zh: 是啊，是啊，那时候叫机器学习。

turns.speaker: Mike Krieger
turns.en: Yeah, it was called machine learning still. And so in shutting it down, you know it when you see it in terms of user growth and traction. And I wasn't expecting Instagram growth, but I was expecting or hoping for or looking for something that felt like at its own legs under it and it could continue to compound. I was really positively surprised by how supportive people were when we announced it. There was a bit of like I told you so which sure anything launching you could be like, "This is not going to work." And you're right, most of the time most things don't work. There was actually very little of that. And most people, the universal reception, at least as I received it, was kudos for calling it when you saw it and not protracted doing this for a long time. (00:42:05): And I've talked to founders since then that have been like, "Yeah, I probably would've taken this thing on for another six months, but saw what you guys did, realized we were barking up the wrong tree, made the call." And I was like, "If that frees up people to go work on a more interesting things, I feel like that's a good legacy for Artifact to have." But for sure there was an ego bruise of is it true that you're only as good as your last game if I am a huge sports fan, right? So is that true or is there something more over a time? I'm very competitive, but primarily with myself and so I'm always trying to find the next thing that I want to go and do that's hard. And unfortunately that probably means that more often than not I'll feel dissatisfied, but the most recent thing that I did, but hopefully that yields good stuff in the end.
turns.zh: 对，当时还是叫机器学习。不过在关停项目时，你一看用户增长和吸引力就知道结果了。我原本没指望能复制Instagram的增长曲线，但我期待、希望、寻找的是那种能自立自强、持续发展的项目。当我们宣布关停时，人们的反应让我很惊喜。倒是有些人幸灾乐祸——毕竟创业项目失败常有。这种情况其实很少见。大多数人的普遍反应，至少我感受到的，是对我们能及时止损的赞赏。（00:42:05）之后我和其他创业者聊过，他们说：“是啊，我可能还会再坚持六个月，但看到你们的决策后，意识到我们方向错了。真佩服你们的果断。”我回应道：“如果这能让更多人去尝试更有趣的事业，那对Artifact来说就是一份不错的遗产。”但不可否认，自负确实受到了打击——就像运动员会想“如果我表现不佳，就说明我江郎才尽了”一样，对吧？但这只是短暂的挫折。说到底，我好胜心很强，但主要是对自己，所以总想寻找下一个挑战。可惜这往往意味着我会感到不满，但希望最终能有所收获。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, I think just the trajectory you went on after shows that it's okay to shut down things that you were working on. Okay, so you mentioned ChatGPT. I wanted to chat about this a bit. So there's something really interesting happening. So on the one hand you guys are doing some of the most innovative work in AI. You guys launched MCP, which is just, I don't know, the fastest growing standard of any time in history that everyone's adopting Claude powered and unlocked centrally the fastest growing companies in the world, Cursor, Lovable, and Bolt, and all these guys. I had them on the podcast and they're all like, "When Claude, I think 3.5 came out, Sonnet, was just like that's made this work finally." (00:43:28): On the other hand, it feels like ChatGPT is just winning in consumer mind share. When people think AI, especially outside tech, it's just like ChatGPT in their mind. So let me just ask you this, I guess first of all, do you agree with that sentiment and then two, as a challenger brand in the AI space, just how does that inform the way you think about product strategy and mission and things like that?
turns.zh: 是啊，我觉得你后续的经历就证明了，有时候放下手头的工作也是没关系的。好的，你刚刚提到了ChatGPT。我想就这个话题聊聊。现在的情况真的很有意思。一方面，你们在人工智能领域做着最具创新性的工作。比如你们推出了MCP，这简直是史上增长最快的标准技术，所有人都采用了Claude技术，还解锁了全球增长最快的公司——Cursor、Lovable、Bolt等。我在播客上采访过他们，他们都说：“当Claude 3.5版本发布时，Sonnet才终于让这一切变得可行。”（00:43:28）另一方面，ChatGPT似乎正在赢得消费者的心。在人们谈论人工智能时，尤其是在科技行业之外，他们脑海中浮现的都是ChatGPT。那么我想先问你几个问题：首先，你是否认同这种观点？其次，作为人工智能领域的挑战者品牌，这是否会影响你们的产品战略、使命规划等方面的思考？

turns.speaker: Mike Krieger
turns.en: Yeah, I mean you look at the sort of public adoption or if you ask people, oh, if you Jimmy Kimmel man on the street kind of thing, name an AI company, I bet they would name and actually I'm not even sure they name open AI, they'd probably name ChatGPT because that brand is the lead brand there as well. And I think that's just the reality of it. I think that when I reflect on my year, I think maybe two things are true. One is consumer adoption is really lightning in a bottle and we saw it at Instagram. So almost maybe more than anybody, I can look internally and say, "Look, we'll keep building interesting products. One of them may hit." But to craft an entire product strategy around trying to find that hit is probably not wise, we could do it and maybe Claude can help come up with a fullness of things, but I think we'd miss out an opportunity in the meantime. (00:44:41): And then instead look yourself in the mirror and embrace who you are and what you could be rather than who others are is maybe the way I've been looking at it, which is we have a super strong developer brand, people build on top of us all the time, and I think we also have a builder brand. The people who I've seen react really well to Claude externally. Maybe the Rick Rubin connection has some resonance here as well. Can we lean into the fact that builders love using Claude? And those builders aren't all just engineers and they're not just all entrepreneurs starting their companies, but they're people that like to be at the forefront of AI and are creating things. Maybe they didn't think of those as engineers, but they're building... I got this really nice note from somebody internal on Anthropic who's on the legal team and he was building bespoke software for his family and connected to them in a new way. (00:45:29): And I was like, "This is a glimmer of something that we should lean into a lot more." And so I think what, and this is actually connecting back to us saying like Claude being helpful here. A lot of what I've been thinking about going into the second half of the year and beyond is how do we figure out what we want to be when we grow up versus what we currently aren't or wish that we were or see other players in the space being. I think there's room for several generationally important companies to be built in AI right now. That's almost a truism given the adoption and growth that we've seen at Anthropic, but also across OpenAI and also places like Google and Gemini. So let's figure out what we can be uniquely good at that place to the personality of the founder. All the things come together, the personality of the founders, the quality of the models, the things the models tend to excel at, which is agentic behavior and coding. (00:46:20): Great. There's a lot to be done there. How do we help people get work done? How do we let people delegate hours of work to Claude? And maybe there's fewer direct consumer applications on day one. I think they'll come, but I don't think that spending all of our time focused on that is the right approach either. And so I came in, everybody expected me to just go super, super hard on consumer and make that the thing and again, would make the other mistake. Instead, I spent a bunch of time talking to financial services companies and insurance companies and others who are building on top of the API. And then lately I've spent a lot more time with startups and seeing all the people that have grown off of that. And I think the next phase for me is let's go spend time with the builders, the makers, the hackers, the tinkerers, and make sure we're serving them really well. And I think good things will come from that and that feels like an important company as we do that.
turns.zh:
是啊，我是说，你看看公众对人工智能的接受度吧——要是你问人们，比如用吉米·鸡毛的街头采访那种方式，提到一家AI公司，我敢打赌他们会说OpenAI，而不是ChatGPT，因为ChatGPT才是这个领域的头牌品牌。我觉得这就是现实情况。当我回顾过去一年时，我觉得有两点是真切的。一是消费者对AI的接受度确实像闪电一样突然，我们在Instagram上就见证了这一点。所以，也许比起任何人，我更能从内部审视自己说：“好吧，我们会继续开发有趣的产品，其中一款可能会成功。”但围绕着这种成功去制定整个产品策略，可能并不明智。我们可以尝试，但Claude或许能帮我们想出更多点子，但与此同时，我们可能会错失良机。（00:44:41）接下来，我觉得关键在于审视自己，接纳真实的自己，而不是模仿他人。比如，我们有非常强大的开发者品牌，人们一直在基于我们的平台开发产品。我认为我们还有建设者品牌。外界对Claude反应很积极。里克·鲁宾（Rick Rubin）的案例或许也有共鸣。我们能否深挖建设者对Claude的喜爱？这些建设者不只是工程师，也不只是创业者，他们是AI领域的先锋，正在创造未来。或许他们不认为自己是工程师，但他们在构建……我收到Anthropic内部法律团队成员的精彩反馈，他为家人开发定制软件，通过新方式与家人保持联系。（00:45:29）我感慨道："这正是我们应该深挖的闪光点。"所以，我的核心思考是——与其模仿其他公司，不如专注自身优势。下半年及未来，我会思考：我们想成为什么样的公司？而非现在所不是、希望成为或看到其他公司正在成为的样子。我认为当下AI领域有空间诞生几家具有代际重要性的公司。鉴于Anthropic、OpenAI、谷歌、Gemini等公司的成功，这几乎是不言而喻的。所以，我们要找到与创始人个性相契合的独特优势。创始人的个性、模型质量、模型擅长的领域（比如自主行为和编程）都要完美契合。（00:46:20）很好。有很多工作要做。比如如何帮助人们高效工作？如何让人们把数小时的工作任务交给Claude？或许第一阶段不会有太多直接面向消费者的应用，但它们迟早会来。不过，我认为把所有精力都投入其中并非明智之举。所以我一上任，大家都期待我大力推进消费者业务，把它作为核心任务，但这又会犯另一个错误。相反，我花了大量时间与金融服务公司、保险公司以及基于API进行开发的初创企业交流。最近，我又与更多初创团队交流，见证了他们借助我们的技术成长壮大。我认为下一步，我要去与建设者、创造者、黑客、发明家们共度时光了。
并且要确保我们能为他们提供优质的服务。我相信这样做定会带来好的结果，而当我们这样做的时候，这家公司也会变得越来越重要。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So essentially it's differentiate and focus, lean into the things that are working, don't try to just beat somebody at their own game.
turns.zh: 基本上就是要做到差异化和专注，专注于那些行之有效的方向，而不是试图在别人的领域与他们竞争。

turns.speaker: Mike Krieger
turns.en: Exactly.
turns.zh: 没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Super interesting. So kind of along those lines, a question that a lot of AI founders have is just like, "Where's a safe space for me to play where the foundational model companies are going to come squash me?" So I asked Kevin Weil this and he had an answer and I noticed looking back at that conversation, he mentioned Windsurf a lot. He was like, "Wow, this kid really loves Windsurf." And then a week later they bought Windsurf. So it all makes sense now. So I guess the question just is, where do you think AI founders should play where they are least likely to get squashed by folks like OpenAI and Anthropic? And also, are you guys going to buy Cursor?
turns.zh: 太有意思了。说到这儿，许多AI创业者都会面临一个问题："哪里才有安全的竞争空间？那些基础模型公司会把我挤出局的！"我曾向凯文·韦尔提过这个问题，他给出了一个答案。回想那次对话，我注意到他多次提到Windsurf。他当时说"哇，这孩子对Windsurf真是痴迷啊"。结果一周后，OpenAI就收购了Windsurf。现在一切都豁然开朗了。所以我想问的是，在你看来，AI创业者应该选择哪个领域，才能最不容易被OpenAI、Anthropic这类巨头压制？另外，你们有计划收购Cursor吗？

turns.speaker: Mike Krieger
turns.en: I don't think we're going to buy Cursor. Cursor is very big, but we love working with them. A few thoughts on this, and it's a question I've gotten. We like to do these kind of founder days with whether it's Menlo Ventures who have about investors and [inaudible 00:48:10]. It's like we've done YC, we've done these founder days, and it's like the question that is on a lot of these founders minds, understandably so. I think things that are going to, I can't promise this as a five to 10 year thing, but at least one to three years, things that feel defensible or durable. One is understanding of a particular market. I spend a bunch of time with the Harvey folks and they showed me some of their UI. I was like, "What is this thing?" And they're like, "Oh, this is a really specific flow that lawyers do, "and you never would've come up with it from scratch and you could argue about whether it's the optimal way they get done things done, but it is the way that they get things done and here's how AI can help with that. (00:48:45): And so differentiated industry knowledge, biotech, I'm excited to go and partner with a bunch of companies that are doing good stuff around AI and biotech and we can supply the models and some applied AI to help make those models go well. And I've been dreaming about at what point does live equipment all get an MCP and that you can then drive using Claude. There's all these cool things to be done there. I don't think we're going to be the company to go build the intent solution for labs, but I want that company to exist and I want to partner with it. Domains like legal, again, healthcare, I think there's a lot of very specific compliance and things. These are things that necessarily sound sexy out the gate, but there are very large companies to go and be built there. So that's number one. Paired with that is differentiated go to market, which is the relationship that you have with those companies, right? (00:49:35): Do you know your customer at those companies? One of our product leads, Michael is always talking about don't just know the company you're selling to, but know the person you're selling to at the company. Are you selling to the engineering department? Because trying to pick which AILM to build on top of or API to build on top of. Let's go talk to them. Is it the CIOs? The CTOs? Is it the CFO? Is it general counsel? So under a company's deep understanding of who they're selling to is the other piece too. What's interesting there is it's probably hard to build that empathy in a three-month accelerator, but you maybe can start having that first conversation and build that out time or maybe you came from that world or you're co-founding somebody who came from that world. Then the last one is like there's tremendous power in distribution and reach to being ChatGPT and having hundreds of millions or billions of users. (00:50:23): There's also people have an assumption about how to use things and so I get excited about startups that will get started that have a completely different take on what the form factor is by which we interface with AI. And I haven't seen that many of them yet. I wanted to see more of them. I think more of them will get created with some things like our new models, but the reason that that's an interesting space to occupy is do something that feels very advanced user, very power user, very weird and out there at the beginning, but could become huge if the models make that easy. And it's hard for existing incumbents to adapt to because people already have an existing assumption about how to use their products or how to adapt to them. So those are my answers. I don't envy them. I would probably be asking those questions if I was starting a company in the AI space. (00:51:10): Maybe that's part of the reason why I wanted to join a company rather than start one. But I still think that there are, and maybe here's fourth, don't underestimate how much you can think and work like a startup and feel like it's you against the world. It's existential that you go solve that problem and that you go build it. It sounds a little cliche, but it's like it's all we had at Instagram. We were two guys and we were like, "Let's see what we can do in an Artifact." We were six people for most of that time and every day felt like it's existential that we get this right, we need to win. And you can't replicate that and you can't instill that with OKRs. You just have to feel it. And that is a way of working rather than a area of building, but it's a continued advantage if you can harness it.
turns.zh:
我觉得我们不会收购Cursor。Cursor规模很大，但我们很喜欢与他们合作。关于这个问题，我有几点看法，也是我常被问到的。我们喜欢参加这类创始人日活动，比如Menlo Ventures为投资者举办的活动（00:48:10）。这类活动中，很多创始人都会有同样的疑问，这完全可以理解。我认为，要想在五到十年内（至少一到三年内）打造出可持续的护城河，关键在于深刻理解特定市场。比如我和Harvey团队交流时，他们向我展示了他们的UI设计。我当时问：“这是什么？” 他们回答：“这是律师特定的工作流程。” 你可能永远想不到这种流程，但这确实是他们的工作方式，而AI可以优化这个流程。（00:48:45）  

在垂直领域的深厚行业知识方面，生物科技领域让我兴奋不已。我们正与许多在AI和生物科技领域表现出色的公司合作，提供模型和应用AI技术，助力他们的研发。我一直在畅想，未来所有实验设备都能接入MCP平台，然后用Claude来操控。这里有无数的创新可能。  

我认为我们不会成为实验室AI解决方案的开发者，但我希望这样的公司存在，并与之合作。法律、医疗等领域同样如此，涉及诸多特定的合规要求。这些领域的创新看似不那么引人注目，但背后有庞大的市场潜力可挖掘。  

与此相伴的是差异化的市场拓展策略，即与客户建立深层合作关系。例如，你要清楚目标客户是谁？是工程部门？还是CIO、CTO、CFO或总法律顾问？深入理解客户需求是关键。这在三个月的加速器项目中很难实现，但至少可以开启对话，为后续合作奠定基础。  

最后，ChatGPT级别的分发和覆盖能力蕴含着巨大能量。（00:50:23）  

还有一些创业公司会提出全新的AI交互界面设计思路，我对此充满期待，但目前这类公司还不多。我希望看到更多类似的创新，尤其是在我们新模型支持下诞生的新生力量。  

这类创新之所以值得关注，是因为它挑战了现有用户的使用习惯，起初可能显得另类甚至怪异，但若模型能让使用门槛降低，市场潜力将不可估量。而现有巨头往往难以适应这种变革，因为人们早已形成固有认知，难以突破思维框架。
使用他们的产品，或者如何适应这些产品。以上就是我的回答。我并不羡慕他们。如果我在AI领域创办公司，可能也会问出同样的问题。（00:51:10）这或许是我选择加入公司而非自己创业的部分原因。但我仍然认为存在这样的情况——或许这就是第四点——别低估自己能像初创公司那样思考和工作，并感觉自己在与整个世界对抗。去解决那个问题，去把它打造出来，这本身就是一种存在感。听起来有些老生常谈，但这正是我们在Instagram时的全部心境。我们当时只有两个人，每天都对自己说："让我们看看能在Artifact平台上做些什么。"在那段日子里，我们始终只有六个人，每一天都觉得必须把事情做好、必须成功。这种紧迫感是无法复制的，也无法用OKR（目标与关键结果）来灌输。你必须亲身感受到它。这是一种工作方式，而非单纯的技术构建，但若能驾驭这种精神，它将成为持续的竞争优势。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that you still have such a deep product founder sense there as you're building products for this very large company now. On the flip side of this, people working with your models and API, so I imagine there's some companies that are finding ways to leverage your models and APIs to their max and are really good at maximizing the power of what you guys have built. And there's some companies that work with your APIs and models that haven't figured that out. What are those companies that are doing a really good job building on your stuff, doing differently that you think other companies should be thinking about?
turns.zh: 我很欣赏你如今在为这家大型公司开发产品时，依然保持着深厚的产品创始人洞察力。另一方面，使用你们模型和API的团队也在不断探索其潜力。我想有些公司已经充分利用了这些资源，而另一些则尚未找到最佳应用方式。那些在模型和API上表现出色的公司，是如何做到与众不同的？其他公司又该如何效仿？

turns.speaker: Mike Krieger
turns.en: I think being willing to build more at the edge of the capabilities and basically break the model and then be surprised by the next model. I love that you cited the companies were like 3.5 was the one that finally made them possible. Those companies were trying it beforehand and then hitting a wall and being like, oh, the models are almost good enough or they're okay for this specific use case, but they're not generally usable and nobody's going to adopt them universally, but maybe these real power users are going to try it out. Those are the companies that I think continuously are the ones where I'm like, "Yep, they get it. They're really pushing forward." We ran a much broader early access program with these models than we had in the past, and part of that was because there's this real, we can hill climb on these evaluations and talk about suite bench and towel bench and terminal bench, whatever, but customers ultimately know Cursor bench which doesn't exist other than in their usage and their own testing et cetera is the thing that we ultimately need to serve. (00:53:29): Not just Cursor but Manus bench, right? If Manus is using our models and Harvey bench, those things and customers know way better than anybody. And so I would say there's two things. One is pushing the frontier of the models and then having a repeatable process. This actually goes back to our summit conversation repeatable way to evaluate how well your product is serving those use cases and how well if you drop a new model in, is it doing it better or worse? Some of it can be classic A/B testing, that's fine. Some of it may be internal evaluation, some of it may be capturing traces and being able to rerun them on with a new model. Some of it's vibes like we're still pretty early in this process and some of it is actually trying it and being one of my favorite early access quotes was the founder heard this engineer screaming next to him. (00:54:14): He was like, "What? This model? I've never seen this before." This is like Opus 4. It was like, "Cool." We're going to engender that feeling and things, but you're not going to be able to feel that unless you have a really hard problem that you're asking the model repeatedly. So those are the things that I think kind of differentiate those companies that are maybe earlier in their journey of adoption versus the later ones.
turns.zh:
我认为关键在于敢于在模型性能边界上突破，勇于接受模型失效的挑战，并从中获得新启发。就像你提到3.5版本最终实现了突破性的成果。那些先行者曾屡屡碰壁，比如模型在特定场景下表现尚可，但缺乏通用适用性，或者仅限于少数核心用户群体。这些公司不断突破边界，始终让我心生敬意。

我们这次模型早期体验计划规模远超以往，部分原因在于客户深知“Cursor Bench”（即用户实际使用场景下的基准测试）才是最关键的衡量标准。（00:53:29）：不仅是Cursor Bench，还有Manus Bench和Harvey Bench等基准测试。客户最熟悉的永远是他们亲身经历的场景，而非抽象的基准数据。

核心在于两点：一是突破模型性能极限，二是建立可重复的评估流程。这直接关联到我们峰会提到的核心理念——通过可重复的评估机制，衡量产品是否真正满足用户需求，模型迭代是否带来实际提升。评估方式可以是经典的A/B测试，也可以是内部评估，或是收集用户行为数据进行再测试。正如早期体验参与者感叹：“工程师旁边尖叫什么？这个模型？我从没见过！”（00:54:14）：这种激动人心的场景正是我们要营造的氛围，但只有当模型真正解决核心痛点时，用户才会产生共鸣。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I can't help but ask about MCP, I feel like that's just so hot and just like Microsoft had their announcement recently where they're like, "That's part of the OS Window." Just what role do you think MCP was will play in the future of product going forward of AI?
turns.zh: 我忍不住要问MCP（微软认知堆栈）的情况。微软近期宣布将其集成到Windows系统中，这无疑是重大进展。你认为MCP在AI产品未来发展中将扮演怎样的角色？

turns.speaker: Mike Krieger
turns.en: I think as the non-researcher in the room, I get to have fake equations rather than real ones in my fake equation. For utility of AI products, it's three part. One is model intelligence, the second part is context and memory, and the third part is applications and UI and you need all three of those to converge to actually be a useful product in AI and model intelligence. We've got a great research team, they're focused on it. There's great, great models being released. The middle piece is what MCP is trying to solve, which is for context and memory. I'll go back to my product strategy example like, "Hey, talk about Anthropic's product strategy," it's going to maybe go out on the web versus here's several documents that we worked on internally and then use MCP to talk to our Slack instance and figure out what conversations are happening and then go look at these documents in Google Drive. The difference between the right context and not. (00:55:44): It's entirely the difference between a good answer and a bad answer. And then the last piece is are those integrations discoverable?
